name: Furby
blurb: Tiger Electronics' talking furry robot pet of 1998, which "learned" English from Furbish
title: Furby: When It Came Out, the NSA Ban and Later Versions
description: Furby is a talking furry robot toy from Tiger Electronics, launched in October 1998 for about $35. It sold millions, was banned by the NSA and is still made.
answer: Furby is an owl-like furry robot toy with big moving eyes and ears that talks, first in its own language, Furbish, and gradually in English. Tiger Electronics, part of Hasbro, launched it in the US on October 2, 1998 for about $35, and it sold more than 40 million in its first three years. Hasbro has relaunched Furby several times since, most recently in 2023, so it is still on sale.

body: The original Furby is about the size of a small owl, covered in fur in many color patterns, with a beak, blinking eyes and ears that move. Light, motion and sound sensors let it react to what is happening around it, and it can be told to "sleep".

A new Furby speaks only Furbish, made of short words and simple syllables, and over time swaps in English words. It does not actually learn what you say; the change is pre-programmed to feel like learning. Two Furbies could talk to each other through an infrared port between their eyes.

body: On January 13, 1999, newspapers reported that the US National Security Agency had banned Furbies from its property, apparently fearing that one could overhear classified conversations and repeat them. The Norfolk Naval Shipyard was also reported to have banned them.

The fear was unfounded: Furby had no ability to record anything, and the words it "learned" were already in its memory. Tiger's president Roger Shiffman said the NSA "did not do their homework" and that "Furby is not a spy."

Yes. Hasbro sells a current Furby, the 2023 generation, in toy shops. Original 1998–2000 Furbies are second-hand and collector items now, and the app-based Furby Connect lost its app support in 2021. In 2025 Furby was a finalist for the National Toy Hall of Fame.

faq.a: Inventors Dave Hampton and Caleb Chung designed it, and Tiger Electronics, a Hasbro company, made and sold it. Hasbro owns the brand today.

faq.q: Did Furby really record what you said?
faq.a: No. The original had no recording ability; its English words were pre-loaded and unlocked over time. The NSA ban rested on a misunderstanding.
About 1.8 million in 1998, 14 million in 1999 and more than 40 million over the original three years of production.
